The P9 Horizon field is a conventional oil accumulation in the Netherlands sector’s P9 blocks. Discovered and developed in the late 1980s/early 1990s, the reservoir delivered oil with associated gas, feeding the Horizon platform’s processing modules and export systems to shore infrastructure.

The Horn Mountain field is located in Mississippi Canyon, Gulf of Mexico, producing from Miocene turbidite sandstone reservoirs. The field is moderate in size and consists of multiple reservoir compartments typical of deepwater channel and fan systems, with additional nearby accumulations tied back to the host.

The West Sole gas field underlies Blocks 48/6 and was the site of the UK’s first offshore gas production beginning in 1967. It produces conventional Rotliegendes sandstone gas in the Southern North Sea and includes satellites like Hoton developed as NUIs tied into the West Sole infrastructure to sustain gas delivery to shore.

The terminal is part of the UK North Sea oil export chain: production flows from offshore platforms via the Forties Pipeline System and onshore processing at Kinneil before storage at Dalmeny and final marine export at Hound Point. There is no local reservoir or upstream production tie-in at the point itself.

The Hyde gas field is part of the West Sole gas accumulation in the Southern North Sea, discovered in the early 1980s. Reservoirs are Lower Permian Leman sandstones, developed via minimum facilities on a normally unmanned platform with production piped to West Sole and onward to the Easington terminal.

The Pierce field lies in the UK-North Sea and produces oil and associated gas via subsea wells tied back to the Hæwene Brim FPSO. Additional satellite production (e.g., Brynhild) has been tied in to optimise reservoir recovery. The field comprises conventional sandstone reservoirs developed with FPSO production infrastructure suited to moderate water depths.

The Indefatigable gas field is a major Permian Rotliegendes sandstone gas accumulation about 100-km northeast of Bacton, discovered in 1966 and first produced in 1971. It spans Blocks 49/18, 49/19, 49/23 and 49/24, containing high-quality reservoir with significant gas volumes developed through multiple platform complexes and subsea tie-backs.

Part of the broader Indefatigable gas field development, AD lies in shallow water over Rotliegendes sandstone reservoir. The field’s development uses multiple jacket platforms and subsea tie-backs to gather gas and condensate, routing through hub facilities to export points. West Inde is a key compartment developed early in the field’s life.

The Indefatigable field’s West compartment sits over Rotliegend sandstone reservoirs, developed with multiple platforms tied into a regional network. Production began in 1971, with AP central to early West Inde operations.

Serving the Indefatigable gas field’s West area, AQ sits above Rotliegend sandstone development blocks. The field’s reservoirs are accessed by multiple wellhead and processing platforms tied into export infrastructure delivering hydrocarbons to onshore terminals.

AT serves the Indefatigable gas field’s central role in the West compartment, handling gas from multiple satellite and wellhead platforms. The field’s Rotliegend reservoir spans several blocks, and AT provides continuity in gas export into UK infrastructure.

Positioned on the Indefatigable field’s West flank, BD accesses Rotliegend gas reservoirs developed as part of an extensive network of platforms and wells delivering gas to export infrastructure via central reception points and pipelines.

BP serves the West Indefatigable reservoir compartment of the Rotliegend gas field, contributing to the integrated development that links multiple platforms and subsea systems to onshore processing terminals.
CD sits within the Rotliegend sandstone Indefatigable gas field, supplying gas to the West Inde cluster tied into export pathways to onshore terminals.
In the Indefatigable field’s West compartment, CP accesses Rotliegend gas reservoirs developed into a multi-platform system that feeds export infrastructure.

The Indefatigable gas field spans several blocks in the Southern North Sea and produces from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Developed since the early 1970s, the field uses multiple bridge-linked platforms and wellhead installations, including Inde D, to deliver gas into regional processing and export infrastructure.

The Independence Hub is located in Mississippi Canyon, Gulf of Mexico, and is associated with multiple gas fields including Atlas, Atlas Northwest, and others. Reservoirs are primarily Miocene-age sandstones. The development is large-scale, designed as a regional gas gathering and export system.

Inspirer is not associated with a single oil or gas field. It is deployed across multiple offshore basins, supporting subsea infrastructure tied to producing fields. Its role is to enable safe and efficient installation and maintenance of subsea equipment in deepwater and harsh environments.

The Ivar Aasen field lies on the Utsira High in the central North Sea. Its reservoirs are Jurassic sandstones containing oil with associated gas. Named after a Norwegian linguist, the field was discovered in 2008 and developed with a conventional fixed platform tied to subsea wells and connected into broader export infrastructure.

The Markham Gas Field was discovered in 1987 and lies across the UK/Netherlands median line in the Southern North Sea. It produces high-pressure natural gas from Triassic/Permian reservoirs, exporting into regional pipeline networks. J6-A functions as a key infrastructure node in the field’s development.

The Jack and St. Malo fields are located in Walker Ridge, Gulf of Mexico, producing from Paleogene (Wilcox) sandstone reservoirs. These are high-pressure, high-temperature reservoirs with significant resource potential, representing large-scale deepwater developments targeting the Lower Tertiary play.

The Jade field sits in Blocks 30/2c (UKCS) and contains high-pressure/high-temperature gas with associated condensate from Triassic sandstones. Discovered in 1996 and commissioned in 2002, it is developed as a satellite tie-back to Judy, with central processing and export to the CATS pipeline and Norpipe system.

The Jasmine field lies in Blocks 30/6 and 30/7a of the Central North Sea with high-pressure, high-temperature gas/condensate reservoirs in Triassic Joanne sandstone. Discovered in 2006, the field achieved first production in November 2013, developed with a WHP and riser/bridge infrastructure tied back to the Judy processing platform.

The Jasmine field lies in Blocks 30/6 and 30/7a of the Central North Sea with high-pressure, high-temperature gas/condensate reservoirs in Triassic Joanne sandstone. Discovered in 2006, the field achieved first production in November 2013, developed with a WHP and riser/bridge infrastructure tied back to the Judy processing platform.

The Johan Sverdrup field is located on the Utsira High in the Norwegian North Sea. It produces oil from Upper Jurassic sandstone reservoirs, primarily the Draupne and Hugin formations. The field is one of the largest discoveries on the Norwegian continental shelf and is developed using multiple fixed platforms with phased expansion.

The Johan Sverdrup field lies in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea on the Utsira High. It is a large oil field producing from Jurassic sandstone reservoirs. Development is based on a hub concept with bridge-linked fixed platforms to enable shared facilities and integrated operations.

The Johan Sverdrup oil field is located in the Norwegian North Sea on the Utsira High. It produces from large, high-quality Jurassic sandstone reservoirs. The field is developed in phases using fixed installations to support long-term, high-volume oil production.

The Johan Sverdrup oil field lies on the Utsira High in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea. Discovered in 2010, it produces oil from Upper Jurassic sandstone reservoirs, mainly the Draupne Formation. It is one of the largest oil discoveries on the Norwegian continental shelf and is developed in multiple phases using fixed platforms.

The Johan Sverdrup field lies on the Utsira High in the central North Sea at ~115-m water depth. Discovered in 2010, it produces oil from Upper Jurassic and associated reservoirs. The multi-platform field centre connects drilling, processing, and riser facilities and represents one of the largest oil developments on the Norwegian continental shelf.

The Jolliet Field lies in the Green Canyon area of the central Gulf of Mexico. Reservoirs are Miocene-age deepwater turbidite sandstones with good porosity and permeability. The field was developed as a moderate-scale deepwater oil project, utilizing subsea wells tied back to the TLP, representing an early application of TLP technology for deeper water Gulf developments.

The Jotun field, discovered in 1994 and starting production in 1999, was developed with Jotun FPSO and a wellhead platform. It produced oil from Paleocene Heimdal Formation sandstones. Production at the original Jotun ceased in 2016; the FPSO was refurbished and redeployed in the Balder area for continued service.

The J-Area fields include Judy, Joanne, Jade and Jasmine accumulations in Blocks 30/7 and 30/6/30/12 of the Central North Sea. Discovered in the 1970s–1990s, these reservoirs produce oil and gas from Palaeocene, Triassic and Chalk sequences. The platform complex was developed as a centralised processing hub with subsea and riser installations tied into Judy.

The K13 gas fields comprise several gas reservoirs in the Southern North Sea discovered in the early 1970s with production from 1975. Reservoirs are Middle Bunter and Rotliegendes sandstones typical of Permian-Triassic stratigraphy. K13A acted as the primary hub receiving gas from satellites. Production from original reserves has ceased, with installations repurposed for transport and compression.

The K12 area forms part of the K7-K12 gas fields in the Southern North Sea, producing conventional gas from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Multiple satellites and hubs, including K12-BD, have been developed to efficiently drain the field.

The K7-K12 gas fields are extensive shallow-water gas accumulations in the Dutch sector, with Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. K12-BP is one of the primary collection points developed to optimize recovery and export.

The K7-K12 gas fields consist of Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs producing conventional natural gas offshore the Netherlands. K12-C serves as one of the processing platforms in the network developed to aggregate and export gas from multiple satellites.

The K12 field is part of the larger K7–K12 gas fields in the Netherlands’ Continental Shelf, producing conventional gas from Rotliegendes sandstones. The field lies offshore northwest of Den Helder in shallow water and has been developed through multiple fixed platforms and subsea completions since the early 1980s. Reservoirs are conventional high-calorific gas with some CO- content.

The K12 gas field development spans blocks in the Southern North Sea producing conventional Rotliegendes gas. Wellhead satellites like K12-D extend reach into reservoir compartments and feed central processing complexes. Field geology consists of Permian sandstones with substantial high-calorific gas reserves developed since the 1980s.

As part of the K7–K12 gas fields, K12-G accesses Rotliegendes sandstone gas reservoirs in shallow offshore Netherlands waters. The field’s development uses multiple satellite and processing installations to optimize reservoir drainage.

K12’s reservoir system consists of Rotliegendes sandstone formations producing conventional gas, developed with numerous wellhead and processing platforms across blocks K7–K12. Satellites like K12-K enhance reservoir coverage.

The K14 field sits in the Southern North Sea’s Block K14 forming part of the larger K14-K18 gas province developed from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. First gas was produced in 1977. The field development comprises a central hub and multiple satellites delivering gas into shared export infrastructure to Dutch gas grids. Rotliegendes reservoirs are conventionally developed at moderate water depths.

The K14 field’s Rotliegendes sandstone reservoir in Block K14 is part of the Southern North Sea’s significant gas province. Installed infrastructure strategically links satellites like K14-FB-1 into central processing hubs to optimize reservoir drainage and export capability into the Dutch gas market.

The K15 field within the K14-K18 gas province produces natural gas from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Production began in 1977. The field is developed as an interconnected cluster with central platforms and satellite installations to maximise recovery. It delivers high-calorific and low-calorific gas into shared export infrastructure to the Dutch continental shelf’s pipeline network.

The K15 field is part of the Southern North Sea’s K14-K18 gas province, producing from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Developed in the late 1970s, the field comprises central production platforms and satellites tied into shared export infrastructure. Its lifecycle reflects mature development across decades.

The K15 field’s Rotliegendes sandstone reservoir in Block K15 is part of the K14-K18 gas fields. Satellites like K15-FC-1 extend reservoir access and feed into central platforms for efficient drainage and export into shared pipeline systems.

Part of the Block K15 development within the K14-K18 gas province, K15-FG-1 collects production from local wells in Rotliegendes reservoirs and sends it to central hubs, supporting shared export infrastructure into the Dutch gas grid.

Situated within the K15 portion of the K14-K18 gas province, the platform gathers conventional natural gas from Rotliegendes sandstone and feeds it into the broader field’s infrastructure for processing and export.

The K17 field, part of the K14-K18 gas province, produces high-calorific gas from Slochteren Formation and Rotliegendes reservoirs. Satellites like K17-FA-1 support field development by extending production reach and tying back into shared infrastructure.

The K01-A Unit field is a shallow-water conventional gas field in the Netherlands sector. It produces gas from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs developed with modest well counts. The field ties into regional infrastructure, with gas exported to larger processing platforms and onward to shore via pipeline networks.

The K2b field is a conventional shallow-water gas accumulation on the Dutch Continental Shelf. Gas is trapped in Rotliegendes or equivalent reservoirs typical of the K7–K12 area. The field has been developed via fixed platforms and flowlines to export networks.

The K04-A field is a shallow conventional gas reservoir in the Dutch sector producing natural gas from Lower Permian formations. Connected with the broader K4b/K5a block developments, the field’s reserves are developed with multiple small platforms and subsea tie-backs feeding central processing.

The reservoir targeted by K4BE is part of the K4b gas accumulations in shallow North Sea waters. These conventional gas reservoirs are developed with multiple unmanned platforms producing to central facilities.

The K5b cluster overlaps with the K05a-B conventional gas field in shallow North Sea waters. Reservoirs produce natural gas from Permian formations, developed through a network of wellheads and platforms feeding central processing.

The K05a-B conventional gas field comprises reservoirs in shallow North Sea waters producing gas from Permian Slochteren formation. The field development includes multiple small platforms tied into a central processing and export network.

The part of the K05a-B gas field associated with K5D consists of conventional shallow-water Permian reservoirs. Development uses small platforms and subsea tie-backs to central processing hubs, with export via trunk pipelines.

The K05/K05a gas fields are conventional offshore gas accumulations in the Netherlands sector, located ~115-km northwest of Den Helder. Discovered in the late 20th century and brought onstream from the early 1990s, these fields produce gas from shallow Permian Rotliegend sandstones. Reservoirs have multiple satellite platforms tied back to central facilities.

The K05/K05a offshore gas fields are conventional shallow-water accumulations in the Dutch North Sea. Reservoirs are primarily Rotliegend sandstones with multiple satellite wellheads feeding central production and export infrastructure. The field was developed in the early 1990s and has remained a stable gas producer via clustered platforms and pipeline networks.

The K05 gas fields produce conventional natural gas from shallow marine sandstone reservoirs. The K05 cluster supports multiple installations with central processing at K5P and satellites like K5EN/C, while K5PK augments production by managing pressures and tie-ins.

The K06-C conventional gas field is a shallow-water Dutch North Sea gas accumulation developed with multiple platforms. Reservoirs are Permian Rotliegend sandstones; production infrastructure includes central processing hubs and satellite nodes such as K6C, tied into one another via subsea pipelines.

The K06 conventional gas fields comprise shallow water gas reservoirs developed since the early 1990s. These reservoirs produce from Rotliegend sandstones, with central facilities and satellite platforms like K6D enhancing field coverage and drainage.

The K06 conventional gas field system includes multiple installations tied to a central hub; reservoirs are Permian shallow water sands developed with central and satellite platforms to optimize field extraction.

The K06 gas field is a conventional natural gas accumulation in the Netherlands sector of the North Sea, developed beginning in 1991. It produces from shallow-water Rotliegend and Zechstein reservoirs typical of Dutch offshore gas geology. The field development includes a central production hub and several satellite platforms including K6GT, K6N and K6P.

The K06 field complex encompasses several conventional gas reservoirs in block K06 of the Dutch continental shelf. These produce from shallow marine sandstone and carbonate sequences typical of Dutch Permian and Triassic stratigraphy. The field includes main production and riser platforms with satellite wellhead platforms like K6N, facilitating reservoir drainage and tie-backs.

The K06 gas field is a producing natural gas field in the Netherlands sector of the North Sea. It produces from conventional shallow marine Rotliegend and Zechstein reservoirs and was brought onstream in the early 1990s. The field’s infrastructure includes a central production hub and multiple satellite wellhead platforms.

The K7 field lies in Block K7 of the Southern North Sea, producing conventional natural gas from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Discovered in 1969 and developed in the late 1970s/early 1980s, it forms part of the K7-K12 cluster of Dutch North Sea gas fields, characterised by high-calorific gas quality and multiple interconnected installations.

The K7 field produces natural gas from Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs within the Southern North Sea. As part of the K7-K12 group, the field is developed through multiple linked platforms and subsea pipelines. Hydrocarbons are collected at satellites like K7-FB and routed to processing hubs such as K7-FA-1 and onward connections to K8 installations.

The K7 field’s Rotliegendes sandstone reservoir is part of the broader K7-K12 gas province. Developed with multiple platforms, gas from K7-FD-1 flows towards the central processing installation (K7-FA-1) before export. The field’s gas quality and reservoir characteristics support extended production life through satellite tiebacks.

The K8 field, in Block K8, produces conventional natural gas from Rotliegendes sandstone, part of the K7-K12 gas province. Discovered circa 1970, the field supports multiple platforms and satellite structures tied to the central K8-FA-1, handling high-calorific gas. Its development reflects early offshore gas exploitation in the Dutch North Sea.

The K8 field is centred on a Rotliegendes sandstone gas reservoir developed with K8-FA-1 as the principal hub. Satellites like K8-FA-2 gather production from wells drilled off the main centre and feed into central processing and export routes, forming an integrated field development.

The K8 field’s geological development is part of the broader K7-K12 gas province. Reservoirs are Rotliegendes sandstones delivering high-calorific gas. Satellites like K8-FA-3 extend reservoir access and tie back to the core K8-FA-1 hub for processing and export.

The K9ab field is part of the broader K7–K12 gas province. It produces conventional Rotliegendes gas through satellite platforms tied into central processing and export routes. Reservoir characteristics mirror other K-block developments in shallow offshore Netherlands waters.

The K9c area sits within the K7–K12 gas field region, exploiting Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Conventional development uses multiple fixed platforms and subsea wells to deliver gas into shared processing systems.
The Katy field lies in Block 44/19b of the UK Southern North Sea producing gas; first gas was achieved in 2013 with field infrastructure tied back to existing systems.

The Kelvin field is a conventional offshore gas accumulation discovered in 2005 in the Southern North Sea. Gas is sourced from Triassic and Carboniferous sandstone reservoirs, with production beginning in 2007 through a subsea tie-back to the Murdoch complex. It is managed within the CMS gas system, which historically gathered and exported production to the Theddlethorpe terminal onshore.

The Kilmar field in Block 43/22a produces conventional Carboniferous gas. Discovered in 1992, production began in 2006 with an NUI platform and tie-in pipelines to Trent. As part of the Tyne, Trent and Tors cluster, production volumes declined, leading to export route closure and field shutdown.

Kings Quay serves fields in the Green Canyon and Walker Ridge areas of the U.S. Gulf of Mexico. Reservoirs are deepwater turbidite sandstones of Miocene age. These fields are developed via subsea wells tied back to the host facility, representing a hub-style development concept for multiple moderately sized accumulations in ultra-deepwater settings.

Kinneil functions as the processing interface between offshore pipeline delivery and onshore export systems. It handles hydrocarbons collected from many North Sea fields transported through integrated pipelines such as the Forties Pipeline System before forwarding stabilised crude to export terminals or refining networks.

The Kittiwake oil field lies in Block-21/18 at about 85–90-m water depth. The field produces Upper Jurassic Fulmar Formation oil and associated gas. With the field’s own production declining, the platform now processes fluids from satellite Goosander, Grouse, Gadwall, Mallard and related areas, collectively known as the Greater Kittiwake Area.

The Kollsnes facility sits near Bergen and receives rich gas through Gassco-operated pipelines from Troll and other Norwegian continental shelf fields. It extracts NGL (ethane, propane, butane, naphtha) for hydrocarbon liquids markets and compresses dry gas for export via Statpipe, Europipe and Zeepipe.

The Kollsnes site is part of the Troll–Kvitebjørn–Visund gas processing chain in the North Sea and Norwegian Sea region. It handles gas landed from Troll and other fields, removes condensate and NGLs, and prepares dry gas for export. Kollsnes supports export networks into Europe, linking to major pipeline systems that carry Norwegian gas to continental destinations.

The Kraka field lies adjacent to the Dan oil field in the Danish sector. Discovered in the late 20th century, it produces from chalk reservoirs with both oil and gas components. It was developed with a small platform and horizontal wells, tying back to Dan for processing.

The Kraken oil field lies in the East Shetland Basin and produces heavy oil from Upper Jurassic sandstone reservoirs. Discovered in 1985, the field is characterized by viscous crude and relatively shallow reservoirs. Development uses subsea wells tied back to a central FPSO with shuttle tanker export.

The Kristin field, discovered in 1997, lies in ~370-m water depth southwest of the Åsgard area. Reservoirs are Jurassic sandstones with high pressure and temperature. It was developed with subsea templates tied back to the central platform. Production includes gas and condensate exported via pipeline systems to onshore facilities.

The Kvitebjørn field, discovered in 1994, lies in the North Sea and produces gas and condensate from deep reservoirs. The development includes integrated platform processing for export via pipelines to onshore gas terminals at Kollsnes (gas) and Mongstad (condensate).

Kårstø handles hydrocarbons from ~30 offshore fields including Statfjord, Åsgard and Sleipner. Its processing trains strip liquids and condense components for storage, with dry gas fed into pipeline networks like Statpipe and Europipe II. Propane and other liquids are exported globally by ship.

The L10 gas field is a large conventional natural gas accumulation in the Southern North Sea, discovered in 1970 and producing since 1976. Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs deliver high-calorific gas; the field acts as a hub for multiple satellite platforms.

Within the L10 gas field, L10-AD accesses Rotliegendes sandstone gas reservoirs. This field has been a major Dutch offshore gas contributor since 1976 and acts as a production and processing hub for the area.

The L10 field’s Rotliegendes sandstone gas reservoirs are accessed from AP via wellheads and satellite tie-ins; production began in 1976 and has continued into the present as part of a multi-platform system.
The L10 field’s gas reservoirs in Rotliegendes sandstones are the production target. The field is a long-lived Dutch offshore gas producer, developed with multiple platforms and subsea ties.
The L10 field produces conventional Rotliegendes gas. Satellite platforms like L10-B enable wide area production with centralized treatment and export via the L10-A hub.
As part of the L10 field, BB accesses Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs; its development augments production capacity by feeding wells into the satellite-to-hub network centered on L10-A.
L10-E taps the same Rotliegendes reservoirs that feed the broader L10 field. This field’s multi-platform architecture supports extensive production and export capacity.

The L10 gas field is a large conventional natural gas field in the Southern North Sea, discovered in 1970 and producing since 1976. Reservoirs are Upper Rotliegendes sandstones on the Dutch continental shelf, developed with multiple wellhead and hub platforms.

The L10 field is a substantial conventional gas accumulation in the Southern North Sea. The reservoir comprises Rotliegendes sandstones producing high-calorific gas tied into Dutch offshore infrastructure.

The installation produces gas from the L10 field’s Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. This field is a major Dutch offshore gas producer with long-term development via multiple platforms and subsea wells.

The L10-M field sits within the broader L10 gas accumulation, producing conventional gas from Rotliegendes reservoirs in shallow Southern North Sea waters. The L10 gas field is a long-lived, multi-platform development.

The L11b-A field lies in the southern Dutch North Sea and produces conventional natural gas (with condensate) from shallow reservoirs. Production began in the 1980s and continues as part of broader L11 and adjacent L8-D developments, feeding regional export infrastructure.

The L13 field is a conventional shallow-water gas accumulation in Block L13 offshore the Netherlands, developed with several fixed platforms feeding gas from Rotliegendes reservoirs. The field comprises L13-FC-1, L13-FD-1, L13-FE-1, with production tied into Dutch export networks.

Operated within the L13 conventional gas field complex, L13-FD-1 accesses Rotliegendes sandstone gas. The field uses multiple fixed platforms to drain reservoir compartments, with gas routed into export pipelines to onshore processing facilities.

The field served by L13-FE-1 is a conventional offshore gas accumulation in Block L13, developed via multiple fixed installations draining Rotliegendes sandstone reservoirs. Gas is collected and exported to onshore facilities.
The L13-FI field lies in Block L13 offshore the Netherlands in shallow water, producing conventional gas from Rotliegendes reservoirs as part of the broader L13 gas development.

The L15 gas field produces conventional natural gas from reservoirs northwest of Den Helder. It was developed in the late 20th century alongside nearby small field infrastructure tying into national export pipelines.

The L2-FA gas field was discovered in 1968 and commenced production via L2-FA-1 in 1992. It produces conventional gas from Rotliegendes reservoirs offshore the Netherlands, with L2-FB later tied back into the platform.

The L4 segment of the L4-L7 gas fields is an established natural gas accumulation in the Netherlands sector of the North Sea, discovered in the 1970s and developed with multiple platforms. Reservoir rocks are Upper Rotliegend sandstones typical of the area. L4A has been a core producing platform for L4 developments since the early 1980s.

The L4-L7 gas fields form a contiguous gas-bearing system in the Dutch North Sea, developed since the 1970s with multiple platforms. Production is primarily from Rotliegend sandstones. L4PN supplements production from the L4 portion of the field, enhancing reservoir drainage.

The L5 block includes conventional natural gas reservoirs in Lower Permian Rotliegendes sandstone beneath the Southern North Sea. The L5-B field was discovered in 1999 and developed with satellite platforms producing natural gas. Nearby fields like L5-C and export hubs support regional development.

The L05-C gas field is a conventional offshore gas accumulation in the Netherlands discovered in 2003 and brought into production by 2006. The reservoir is Rotliegendes sandstone, typical of Southern North Sea gas fields, and has proven extractable gas reserves in the low billions of cubic meters.

The L5-FA field produces conventional natural gas from reservoirs offshore northwest of Den Helder. It was developed alongside other small fields and integrated into the national pipeline network (NOGAT) for export to onshore treatment plants.

The L5a-D field is a deep, high-pressure gas accumulation in the Dutch sector. Production includes gas (via L5a-D4 and other wells) with flows transported through offshore infrastructure into national export routes.

The L6-B field is a small natural gas prospect in ~30–35-m water depth on the Netherlands Continental Shelf. Gas is produced from shallow Permian or Slochteren Formation sandstones typical of the Southern North Sea and exported via subsea pipeline to L8-P4 for processing and onward transport.

The L8P area is within the L8 block of the Southern North Sea, a gas-bearing region developed for hydrocarbon production from Permian and Slochteren Formation sandstones. Production from fields in the area has historically been exported via subsea pipelines to onshore processing and transmission systems.

The installation draws hydrocarbons from small, high-calorific natural gas reservoirs within Block L8 and adjacent acreage on the Netherlands Continental Shelf. The gas is characteristic of Rotliegend/Slochteren sandstone reservoirs typical of the Southern North Sea.

The L9 field is a conventional offshore gas complex north of Den Helder, developed with multiple platforms including L9-FA-1, L9-FB-1, and L9-FF-1. Reservoirs are Rotliegendes sandstones characteristic of southern North Sea gas fields.
Part of the L9 field development, L9-FB-1 accesses Rotliegendes gas reservoirs and contributes to L9 area production tied into the Nogat/NGT system.

The L9 field produces conventional gas from Rotliegendes reservoirs. As one of the larger installations in the sector, L9-FF-1 serves as a central production and partial processing hub linking satellite flowlines to export networks.

The Lancelot complex serves the Lancelot gas field in the Southern North Sea, developed in the early 1990s with first gas in 1993. Reservoirs are conventional Rotliegend sandstone, producing predominantly dry gas with some condensate. The field sits about 53-km offshore and is a regional hub receiving tie-backs from satellite accumulations including Guinevere, Excalibur and others.

Part of the Leman gas field, a Permian Rotliegendes sandstone dataset in the Southern North Sea discovered in 1966. The field produces dry gas that is routed to central processing hubs like Leman Alpha and onward to the Bacton Gas Terminal.

The Leman gas field lies in Blocks 49/26 and 49/27 of the Southern North Sea, discovered in 1966 with production commencing in 1968. The reservoir comprises Rotliegendes sandstone at ~6,000 ft depth with large gas volumes (~11 Tcf original gas in place). Development involved numerous platforms tied back to central complexes with export to Bacton.

AD serves the Leman gas field’s Rotliegendes reservoir, routing production gas through the Alpha hub. High reservoir continuity in Rotliegendes sands ensures integration across multiple AD subsections.
Supports Rotliegendes Sandstone gas production in Leman Block 49/26, routed to central facilities for export.
